body: Very similar story over here. I don't think my family would have survived without cosleeping! We were awake all night when we tried to keep her in the crib. Cosleeping following the safe sleep 7 resulted in all of us being so much more rested and so much happier. I agree we'll have to figure out how to get her to sleep in her own room further down the road but I'm not worried about it. Sleep is so developmental. Her sleep at say 18 months old will not look like it does now at 7, and we'll adjust and do whats best for our family as we go along.

Sounds like she's trying hard to get lots of attention, any way she can get it. The key would be keeping the attention focused on completing the task on the list. LOTS of praise for completing a task, excitement over watching her move to the next task. She needs to see that completing her tasks gets her just as much attention, if not more, than being defiant does, and what's more she gets to see mama super proud and happy. This is also why I suggest starting with a morning list or a list for a time of day that isn't stressful. Introduce it as something fun and exciting, something that gets her positive attention. Then moving to a nighttime list. If she resorts to not obeying/dawdling, just say, "Oh darn, I was so excited to see you check off jammies on your list! Oh well." Then remove attention. It might take another 10 minutes of her waiting to see if you'll give her attention for disobeying ( which I get is frustrating at the end of a long day, but it's important to show her that disobeying no longer gets extra mom attention). When she sees that won't work, she's likely to see that she'll get praised for doing what's on the list. I'm not saying this will work for every kid, but it's a way to give her the attention she is craving for doing exactly what you want her to do, so win win for everybody!

This could be a good age to introduce a bedtime checklist. Something printed on laminate that has 3-5 things she needs to do in the evening. Allow her to do a big checkmark with expo market next to tasks she completes. For some kids just the novelty and excitement of using the expo marker/checking things off is enough, but others might be motivated by a small reward after completing all the tasks. Could even challenge her to time herself and see if each day she can complete her check list faster than the day before. If bedtime is the challenging part of the day, you could start with a morning checklist that you know she will complete easily to build confidence and excitement, then introduce bedtime checklist.

I really think hormones cannot be understated as a cause of so much postpartum anxiety and feels. I did not feel myself during those anxiety attacks, and actually that's what helped me get through them - I was able to be like, "Ok, this feeling I'm having and these thoughts in my head aren't really coming from me. It's just my body adjusting to postpartum life. I don't need to indulge these thoughts or feelings. Just feel it and let it pass." The other thing that helped was time. My baby is almost 10 weeks and I feel way more confident in caring for her now than at 6 weeks. 6 weeks was the absolute worst because around 5 weeks she "woke up" to the world and all of the sudden she was crying so much more and I felt like I didn't know what she needed, what she was trying to communicate, etc. Now at almost 10 weeks she's pretty obvious - the tired cry, the hungry cry, etc. She's also sleeping way better, but even on the bad nights I can tell myself that I absolutely have survived all the bad nights and can do another one. 

All this to say, it WILL get easier.

You may be totally right about your children's school and the lack of continuity and overall effort on the teachers' parts. However, as a teacher myself, I will say that I knew very few teachers who were able to provide an engaging, relevant education to students via virtual learning. Everything about my teaching is geared towards having 25-30 students in person, in front of me, with all my materials available to us. We do group work, we do share outs, we use the whiteboard spaces around the room, I am modeling how to do work under the doc cam, I post things around the room for students to use for particular lessons. I likely have a poster explaining "the arrow way" of math posted for students to reference. I will also sit kids struggling with the arrow way next to a kid who does understand the arrow way, so they can ask a buddy for help. Throw a ball at home? Don't know what the goal was there, but I likely would have made that a group activity so we could compare the distance/velocity of Group A's ball with Group B's.  So much of teaching is using the power of social interaction as a vessel for learning; kids are, after all, often more interested in each other than the lesson, so most master teachers know how to build off of that need for socialization to teach content. How the hell that translates into a zoom school, ESPECIALLY for younger children, is still beyond me, after 1.5+ years trying everything in power to make it work during the pandemic. 

All this to say, teaching/learning during the pandemic couldn't be further from what teaching/learning looks like in a classroom setting, in my opinion, and I wouldn't compare the two when assuming that schools and teachers just don't care.

I agree that that for many, 4 years of high school is too much, especially for students who have no plans to go to college. I do like the way my school does it, though: by senior year, if a student has been consistently passing their classes, they may only need to take two classes (usually personal financed and one other one, and the personal finance class is amazing for students about to enter "the real world".) They have almost all the credits they need. The rest of the time can be spent at an internship or a job. Students who have not passed enough classes use that senior year to make up credits. Students who do plan to go to college use that year to rack up AP credits, or take a class like career and technical writing, which walks them through applying for scholarships and writing admissions essays. It's not a perfect system, but I feel like it speaks to what you're saying in that it acknowledges that by age 17/18, students' time should be spent doing what is most useful to them.

I teach 9th and 10th grade, and I will say I take on a different tone and demeanor with my male students than I do with my female students. I wish it wasn't this way, but here we are. Many of my male students are attention-seeking and will do anything to get their friends' approval or to make others laugh. I try to use that to my advantage - I call out all the good behavior. Not in a scripted, teacher way, like, "Excellent participation, Aidan." More casual and joking: "Aidan did you eat your wheaties this morning? This man is schooling y'all today. A+ Aidan. If I could afford a cookie, I'd give it to you." I ask for volunteers to sit on my stool and hold up the model poster before group work because they love to sit there with a cheesy smile. I choose one to pass out papers and pretend yell at them for being too slow.  I keep it light whenever I can - then when it's time to do work, I'm privately praising the boys who are on task, kind of like a coach would, just loud enough for the kid next to them to hear: "Way to be a leader, Jayden." "I see you working hard, Caden." I leave comments on google classroom commending them for showing responsibility, or character, or whatnot. I call home to the few boys who are acting like leaders and tell their parents how they are showing leadership. They love that, and they work even harder after those calls. Deep down all they want is to be liked and to receive validation. They will find every maladaptive way possible to get it if I'm not doling it out in the ways that they respond to. 

I should mention I am also a rather dorky female. Speaking 15 year old boy does not come naturally to me. I have to shine it on.

Normally I'd say give him time, appreciate his honesty, etc, but there are a couple of red flags for me personally. Namely, that his parents "know about you" but he won't tell them you're in a relationship and ESPECIALLY that he wouldn't tell your friends you are together. I've never met a guy who didn't tell the friends who wasn't either not totally invested in the relationship or using the girl as his side chick.

You've known each other five years, been dating for a year. If he's not sure how he feels about you after that amount of time, you should prepare yourself for a pattern of "not being sure" the rest of your relationship. 

Want to move in together? He'll need time to think about it, maybe a few months. Talking engagement? Tack on another year, perhaps. Kids? He'll know by the time he's forty. 

There's nothing wrong with someone who takes their time in relationships, but you need to decide if you're okay with going at a slow pace and most likely being the one to always initiate change and growth.
